rv.q: A wonderfully generous, uplifting piece of theatre.
Together with its lovely movement, the show becomes unstoppably winning, ineffably exuberant.
Some weaknesses are exposed. Hawley's marvellous songs are more planted than propelling. Lynne Page's choreography is, well, pedestrian.
It’s a hugely admirable achievement, and if it left me personally a bit cold – and I’m very possibly the only one! – I couldn’t help but be impressed.
You’d need a heart of stone not to be moved by this generous portrait of humanity: a true homegrown triumph.
A city loved by its people – and if this superb musical is anything to go by, with very good reason.
Her writing and Richard Hawley's protean music are gorgeously balanced.

The company of actor-singers ... get to the pulsing heart of the stories, Rachael Wooding all busy Yorkshire common sense as Rose, Alex Young all anxiety as Poppy, determined to continue telling herself that everything is fine until mere repetition makes it so.
Bush and Hawley have written a heartfelt love letter to a city that at times in its history has been neglected and unloved.
This is a mega-budget muddle posing as a state-of-the-nation musical.
It's a joyful, gritty show with fire in its heart.
But it is to say that that this musical amounts to less than the sum of its parts.

cn.t: Critics are sharply divided on this Sheffield-set musical triptych spanning decades in a brutalist housing estate. Most praise Bush's evocative storytelling and powerful sense of place, though one dismisses it as heavy-handed political propaganda.
